scenarioStory.history: 42-year-old male with longstanding Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Omnipod insulin pump on right upper arm). Wife states he completed a 45-minute morning run at 0700, came inside acting 'fine,' then about 20 minutes ago became progressively confused, sweaty, and restless. He isn't making sense, won't sit down when she asks, and is now wandering around the kitchen. Wife denies any drug or alcohol use; she states 'he's never been like this.' She thinks he skipped breakfast after the run. The pump 'beeped earlier' but she doesn't know what the alarm was.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: Crew arrives to find PD on scene with a 42-year-old male wandering the kitchen, diaphoretic, restless, and confused. Wife reports sudden onset 20 minutes ago after a morning run. Patient is not verbally aggressive or threatening — he just isn't making sense and doesn't follow directions well. NOTE: While he seems confused, he is still able to somewhat follow orders if the providers start talking to him and give him simple instructions (e.g., 'come sit down here'). He will sit when asked, though he may need prompting again. There are subtle medical tells available to the observant clinician: profuse diaphoresis, an insulin pump on the right upper arm, and a medical alert bracelet for Type 1 Diabetes. → Hypoglycemia identified: Glucose comes back at 38 mg/dL. The clinical picture now resolves: this is symptomatic hypoglycemia presenting as confusion, not a primary behavioral emergency. Patient remains confused and restless — too confused to reliably swallow oral glucose. Because he will sit and follow simple instructions with calm coaching (and his wife's help), an IV may be obtainable; if so, IV dextrose (D10 preferred) is the protocol treatment. If he keeps pulling his arm away and IV access cannot be established, glucagon IM is the protocol alternative. Either is acceptable. → Dextrose or glucagon given: Dextrose or glucagon has taken effect. Patient is now oriented x4, embarrassed by his behavior, and cooperative. Glucose now ~92 mg/dL. He is asking what happened. Crew can now establish IV access if not already in place, give PO complex carbs, and transport for evaluation. Per protocol he should be transported because symptoms were severe and pump malfunction is suspected.

patientInformation.patientCondition: Confusion and restlessness, acting 'not himself' for the past 20 minutes

scenarioEvents.name: Initial Contact
scenarioEvents.description: Crew arrives to find PD on scene with a 42-year-old male wandering the kitchen, diaphoretic, restless, and confused. Wife reports sudden onset 20 minutes ago after a morning run. Patient is not verbally aggressive or threatening — he just isn't making sense and doesn't follow directions well. relatedChecklist: Confirm scene safety with PD; assign partner to safety/egress
Consider medical causes before labeling 'behavioral' (AEIOU-TIPS)
Attempt verbal reassurance / de-escalation from a safe distance
Get history from wife: diabetes, insulin pump, skipped meal, onset
Note diaphoresis, insulin pump on arm, medic-alert bracelet
Obtain finger-stick blood glucose (result: 38 mg/dL)

scenarioEvents.name: Hypoglycemia identified
scenarioEvents.description: Glucose comes back at 38 mg/dL. The clinical picture now resolves: this is symptomatic hypoglycemia presenting as confusion, not a primary behavioral emergency. Patient remains confused and restless — too confused to reliably swallow oral glucose. Because he will sit and follow simple instructions with calm coaching (and his wife's help), an IV may be obtainable; if so, IV dextrose (D10 preferred) is the protocol treatment. If he keeps pulling his arm away and IV access cannot be established, glucagon IM is the protocol alternative. Either is acceptable.
relatedChecklist: Defer oral glucose — patient unable to safely protect airway/cooperate
D10 IV in 100 mL (10 g) increments to mental status, max 250 mL (25 g) — OR glucagon 1 mg IM if no IV
Have wife stop/disconnect the insulin pump
Apply SpO2 and cardiac monitor as patient tolerates
Reassess vitals, mental status, and repeat glucose after dextrose/glucagon

scenarioEvents.name: Dextrose or glucagon given
scenarioEvents.description: Dextrose or glucagon has taken effect. Patient is now oriented x4, embarrassed by his behavior, and cooperative. Glucose now ~92 mg/dL. He is asking what happened. Crew can now establish IV access if not already in place, give PO complex carbs, and transport for evaluation. Per protocol he should be transported because symptoms were severe and pump malfunction is suspected.
relatedChecklist: Establish IV access if not already obtained
Offer 25 g oral glucose / complex carbs once airway protected
Transport — pump malfunction suspected, refusal criteria not met
Document glucose values, dextrose/glucagon given, pump status, mental-status trend

scenarioEvents.name: IM sedative given, no glucose check
scenarioEvents.description: Crew misread the scene as substance-use or pure behavioral and gave IM ketamine 4 mg/kg or IM midazolam 5 mg without ever checking glucose. Patient is now deeply sedated, but the underlying hypoglycemia is uncorrected and progressing. Sedation is masking the metabolic crisis. Respiratory drive is depressed, glucose continues to fall.
relatedChecklist: Recognize miss — get the glucose NOW (result: 32 mg/dL)
Open airway, apply O2, assist ventilations with BVM as needed
IV D10 — start with 100 mL of 10% dextrose, titrate to mental status
Stop / disconnect the insulin pump immediately
Expedite transport; notify receiving facility of iatrogenic over-sedation + hypoglycemia
